packet.headline_seed: Is hojicha the next matcha? The Japanese tea creeping onto menus
packet.description_seed: From lattes to ice-cream, Japanese hojicha tea has been creeping onto menus across the UK.

what: Is hojicha the next matcha? The Japanese tea creeping onto menus

clean_source_blocks.text: From lattes to ice-cream, Japanese hojicha tea has been creeping onto menus across the UK.

Browsing through the menu in a London cafe, Ana Costa wasn't sure what drink she was in the mood for. She didn't fancy a coffee and was considering a matcha latte, when hojicha caught her eye. A Japanese drink made from green tea, hojicha is dry-roasted at high temperatures to produce a distinctive aroma and nutty flavour. It's less bitter than green tea, with a low caffeine content - and it's creeping onto café menus. Hojicha tea has always been on the menu, in its traditional form, at chef Shuko Oda's Koya restaurant in London. "Traditionally, we don't put milk or any sugar or sweetenings in with hojicha," Oda says. "It's meant to be a brown, clear tea that is very much an every and any time of the day type of hot drink."

Across the country, matcha is ubiquitous in specialty drinks and desserts. It even works its way into some savory dishes. But it isn’t the only type of Japanese green tea powder that chefs are experimenting with in restaurants. In the last few years, hojicha has crept onto dessert menus from Los Angeles to New York City. The roasted green tea, derived from discarded leaves and stems of the same type of tea plant harvested for matcha, is less expensive and has less caffeine than its ultra-popular counterpart. Its smooth, nutty taste and smoky aroma offer a distinctive flavor profile that sings when paired with classic ingredients like seasonal fruit, chocolate, and espresso.

The tea even hit the menu for the first time at east London coffee roasters Grind this summer, in the form of a black sesame hojicha. Head of coffee Howey Gill says it added the drink after keeping an eye on Japanese food and drink trends spreading to the UK - though he acknowledges the brown colour is "not as sexy as matcha". Ana, 21, says her hojicha latte from How Matcha - served iced with oat milk and a pump of vanilla syrup - is definitely "less Instagrammable" than matcha, but she enjoys the flavour and says the appearance doesn't matter to her. Shoppers carrying cups of bright green matcha have become ubiquitous in town centres across the UK. As of February, even Greggs is selling it.

original_article.research:
[Lähde: BBC World]
Browsing through the menu in a London cafe, Ana Costa wasn't sure what drink she was in the mood for. She didn't fancy a coffee and was considering a matcha latte, when hojicha caught her eye.

A Japanese drink made from green tea, hojicha is dry-roasted at high temperatures to produce a distinctive aroma and nutty flavour. It's less bitter than green tea, with a low caffeine content - and it's creeping onto café menus.

Hojicha tea has always been on the menu, in its traditional form, at chef Shuko Oda's Koya restaurant in London.

"Traditionally, we don't put milk or any sugar or sweetenings in with hojicha," Oda says. "It's meant to be a brown, clear tea that is very much an every and any time of the day type of hot drink."

But Oda says she's seeing the drink pop up more and more across the UK, largely in milky hojicha lattes and desserts, and even added hojicha ice cream to her own restaurant's menu earlier this year.

At matcha chain Jenki, iced hojicha latte sales were 55% higher across its six London cafes between January and April than during the same time period the previous year.

Meanwhile Rashique Siddique, director of How Matcha, says hojicha latte sales have "grown significantly" over the past year, with How Matcha now selling one or two cups for every five matcha lattes it sells.

"Hojicha feels like where matcha was two or three years ago," Siddique says, "it's moving from niche to mainstream quite quickly."

The tea even hit the menu for the first time at east London coffee roasters Grind this summer, in the form of a black sesame hojicha. Head of coffee Howey Gill says it added the drink after keeping an eye on Japanese food and drink trends spreading to the UK - though he acknowledges the brown colour is "not as sexy as matcha".

Ana, 21, says her hojicha latte from How Matcha - served iced with oat milk and a pump of vanilla syrup - is definitely "less Instagrammable" than matcha, but she enjoys the flavour and says the appearance doesn't matter to her.

Shoppers carrying cups of bright green matcha have become ubiquitous in town centres across the UK. As of February, even Greggs is selling it.

And increasing numbers of people are buying the powder to prepare at home, too.

The quantity of powdered matcha sold at UK supermarkets and convenience stores has grown more than fourfold over the past year, with shoppers spending nearly £9m on it over the last 12 months, according to data from research company Nielsen IQ.

[Lähde: AOL]
Across the country, matcha is ubiquitous in specialty drinks and desserts. It even works its way into some savory dishes. But it isn’t the only type of Japanese green tea powder that chefs are experimenting with in restaurants.

In the last few years, hojicha has crept onto dessert menus from Los Angeles to New York City. The roasted green tea, derived from discarded leaves and stems of the same type of tea plant harvested for matcha, is less expensive and has less caffeine than its ultra-popular counterpart. Its smooth, nutty taste and smoky aroma offer a distinctive flavor profile that sings when paired with classic ingredients like seasonal fruit, chocolate, and espresso.

“One of the things we like about hojicha is that it’s relatively cheap [compared to matcha],” says Klementine Song, chef de cuisine at Tsubaki in Los Angeles. Hojicha is almost five times less expensive than the matcha that the restaurant uses.

Since its opening in 2017, the modern Japanese izakaya has offered a hojicha soft-serve parfait that’s remained fairly popular. Currently, the hojicha parfait comes topped with a burnt miso caramel and candied walnuts coated in cornflake dust.

Related: 13 Delicious Ways to Eat and Drink Matcha

In addition to the affordability of the ingredient, Song appreciates hojicha for its “extra roasty, caramel” flavor, which she likens to coffee or barley tea. That unique smokiness comes from a manufacturing process that dates to the 1920s, when tea merchants in Kyoto began collecting the leftover tea plant trimmings and roasting them over charcoal.

Matcha, by comparison, was invented more than 1,000 years ago in China. It was then further developed in Japan.

Across town, Harry Posner takes a more labor-intensive approach with hojicha at Tomat, the British-inspired, farm-to-table restaurant he owns and operates with his wife and business partner, Natalie Dial.

Rather than buying pre-roasted green tea powder, the lead chef roasts and grinds his hojicha using organic sencha leaves, the kitchen’s wood-fired grill, and one “very large” donabe, or Japanese earthenware cooking pot.

During fall and winter, Posner uses the powder to flavor ice cream, which is then finished with cubes of instant espresso jelly and a black sesame tuile. The restaurant also serves an ultra-smoky hojicha latte during daytime service.

[Lähde: Palo Alto Weekly]
It’s a matcha lover’s paradise at Palo Alto’s newest drink and dessert spot, Maruwu Seicha.

From matcha lattes adorned with fluffy “snow top” to gelato made with ceremonial grade matcha, Maruwu Seicha’s menu boasts a variety of tea-forward treats. The Kyoto-based company has been producing matcha out of its tea farm in Uji, Japan, since 2011 and operates a dozen retail locations throughout the country. Maruwu Seicha opened its first international outpost in San Francisco’s Japantown last year, and on Oct. 20, it soft opened a new cafe in downtown Palo Alto.

A post shared by Peninsula Foodist (@peninsulafoodist)

“The brand is really focused on quality tea and spreading the (Japanese) culture,” said Peng Chen, who is part of the operation management team for Maruwu Seicha USA.
